utterances.text: Okay. And in the term -- in the -- in the words in the top, the secretariat of the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As was correctly noted by Mr. Gosnell, and I agree with him, this is a, to date, unique case in which we see this term being used. I do not see this term, "secretariat of the president," in other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the -- what is the term in -- in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the term in B/C/S as it appears in this document is "sekretarijat predsednika," secretariat of the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So just to clarify the president's -- or to take one step further the president's question, the similarity in translation is between the term "prime minister" and "president"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to avoid any confusion because, for example, in the translation of this particular document, I think we have a suboptimal translation. It says "government president." A government president does not mean anything in English. The correct term would be either president of the government or prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the anomalous aspect of this -- or the heading of this document is that this is the only document that says either the secretariat of the president or the secretariat of the prime minister; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another subject that is mentioned in you previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And could we have 65 ter 1028 which is Prosecution tab 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And during your testimony at page 2510, you said that: "Arkan was supported by very significant powers in Belgrade and that he was untouchable." Now would you agree with me that at least as of the 21st of September, 1991, and given your review of the documents, it's not very likely that anything Goran Hadzic could have done would have made Arkan untouchable; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find that a very difficult question to respond to. First let me make it clear that it was -- what you quoted from page 2510 was I believe my perception that -- or my observation that it was the general perception in the area that Arkan was supported by very significant powers in Belgrade and that he was untouchable, and it is true that when the military or other authorities refer to the power of Arkan, the aura of untouchability, as it were, that surrounded him, they do generally not tend to refer to that aura existing because of association with Mr. Hadzic but rather to the view that he was supported by authorities in Belgrade, in particular the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 71 of the document on the screen. And this is the 194th SFRY Presidency minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at this stage can you remind you what is General Panic's position?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular point in time, if memory serves, he was the Chief of Staff I believe. I'm not entirely certain on -- on a particular date here, but I believe he was the Chief of Staff of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree that he might have been the commander of the 1st Military District at this stage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could also be true. Again, I'm not an expert on military positions at this point in time. But I do refer to this -- Mr. Panic's, or General Panic's, participation in the SFRY Presidency in paragraphs 205 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes. And this is where you refer to Mr. Panic, General Panic saying that Hadzic suns Arkan like some body-guard; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That's what I have stated. He then goes on: It is necessary to ask Hadzic and tell him to remove that Arkan from that area. And he also mentioned that he had discussed this topic with Mr. Milosevic who was doing, quote/unquote, everything to help resolve the problem. I should note that Mr. Panic, despite concerns about Arkan's activities at this time, also noted, as I state in paragraph 205, that the military had earlier accepted Arkan and thought that he had been carrying out tasks that were of a positive nature, which perhaps also explains why General Biorcevic saw fit in November 1991 to award Arkan with a trophy weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, what I'd like to do is put General Panic's word in a broader context as they appear in these minutes. And what we see, I believe, on page 71 -- I'm just trying to find the exact start of the passage. Well, let me read it out. And I don't see the exact start, but this is quoted in your report. And this is General Panic saying: "We also must have a serious showdown with Arkan and the White Eagles and all those who are destroying what we are trying to do today. Arkan is led by Hadzic. I was in Knin yesterday, and they were all wondering in way or another what Arkan was doing in the area. He has brought with him as some sort of body-guard. We should call President Hadzic and tell him to remove Arkan from the area. This young man probably wants to prove himself in some way. You know yourselves that he is an international criminal and that he cannot hold this position. While he is good, it is okay to keep him, but when is he not good anymore, he should be removed. This also goes for Jovic." Now if we can skip to page 73 of the English. Let's -- it's actually enumerated at the bottom as page 70. And in this case, it's Borisav Jovic speaking. And Borisav Josic says: "As for these Eagles and Arkan, I think that the army should arrest them pursuant to our order." And then Panic responds: "MUP should do that." And Borisav Jovic says: "No, that is not the starting point. Our position here is that nobody should be expelled." And then he goes on. And then if we skip down to the middle of page -- what is enumerated as page 71, Jovic says: "We did not prevent them from fighting against the Ustashas but we forbid them from expelling innocent people, that's the point." And he goes on at the bottom of the page to say: "So if the army could take up this task, I would gladly assign this task to it, and if they catch him -- if they catch them in the act, they should disarm then and arrest them. Why do they need weapons there ..." And then Panic responds on the next page: "There is no task that the army cannot accomplish as long as the Supreme Command orders it. If the Supreme Command orders us to move out of Bosnia tomorrow, we will do it very simply. We will declare a state of alert and turn our back across the Drina. If we get such an order, we will carry it out." Now just to pause there, reading that response by Panic, do you see that he is -- let me just put it like this. Do you think that Panic's response means that he wants to go along with such an order or is he saying, Well, you can give us any order you want but that would be catastrophic? Or not desirable, let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see how you could arrive at that reading of Panic's comments, but I also think that requires a rather high level of reading into read his, the subtext, if you will, or is presumed subtext of what he is saying. I think the significant thing is, and you read it aloud a little bit earlier, is Panic's initial response which is MUP should do that. I mean, Arkan is a -- is a hot potato, mind you a hot potato that they have themselves created, sponsored, armed, et cetera, and financed, who has now become undesirable, and they're basically passing this around the table. No one seems to want to take responsibility for shutting Arkan down, as it were. And, of course, unfortunately, the historical record shows that Arkan remained active in that area until well into the mid-1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at the bottom of page 72, as it's enumerated, Kostic says: "Zivota, at a session here I once asked what was the relationship between Arkan and the JNA, and you were the one who told me that he was a good." Jovic says: "In matters of war." Kostic says: "We should avoid any major clashes now. This should be done in a nice way so that these lads of his can stay, if they want, in the army." Panic: "Arkan carried out missions in the area very efficiently. At one point he broke away, but they brought him back, et cetera. However, he is doing Yugoslavia a disservice. He should be called and given a task. Those who sent him there should call him. I do not know who sent him. However, Arkan was present in Bijeljina, Zvornik, around Sarajevo, Knin et cetera. Someone is leading him and issuing tasks to him. We should see who is doing this. It is certain that it is not us. "Arkan is very disciplined when performing tasks. However, his patrons should be the ones to call him." When you read this -- well, let me just ask you generally: What do you think is going on here? Why is Panic -- how is Panic responding? And I couldn't agree with you more in your description of this as a hot potato. Do you think Panic is speaking at face value or do you think that he has a close association with Arkan and is attempting to un -- understate it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I would just like to point out that in the first passage you read, the quote was -- in the B/C/S he says, "Here once I asked what the relationship between Arkan and the JNA and was and you were the one who told me that he was good," not "a good." And in response to your question, there's, again, a clear indication that the army knows who Arkan is. I have a document somewhere in the report from 1982, I believe, almost ten years before this meeting takes place, in which they already knew at that point in time that Arkan was a career criminal who had, in fact, also done a very unpatriotic thing of avoiding compulsory military service in socialist Yugoslavia. So there was no beating around the bush in terms of Arkan was. What I read Panic as saying here, and it's significant to me that he's having this discussion with Borisav Jovic, who is very proximate to Slobodan Milosevic, to me the subtext here is you, the political leadership and the police - which is very much seen as a rival by the military - you unleashed this person and for a while we all agreed that this was desirable. As long as he was helping us with what we deemed to be patriotic and noble activities of asserting our control over that area of Yugoslavia, we were all on the same page and so far so good. But lately he has become a problem and you created this problem so you should clean it up. That is what the military is saying to the civilian leadership because they know -- everyone around this table knows that the State Security Service is not under the control of the military but is rather under the control of the political leadership of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you think the military is saying that to the civilian authorities or do you think the civilian authorities are saying that to the military? And I say that because we have Jugoslav Kostic saying, "Zivota, at a session here, once I asked you what was the relationship between Arkan and the JNA," and you've helpfully corrected the rest of th translation, the point being that Kostic's view appears to be, as reflected here, that Panic had something to do with at the very least blessing his involvement in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I again think that the point is slightly more narrow than that. I think what is going on here is that they are saying at one point you, the military, had no problems with Arkan, and we were all agreed that Arkan's presence out there was desirable and that what he was doing was for the common good. That time has passed. And I think the civilian leadership is chiding Panic, if you will, and saying perhaps there's a bit of hypocrisy involved in suddenly him turning around and saying no, this person is a criminal. But as is clear from the comments here several times, and again this is borne out by many other documents, they all knew, if we go a year back in time before Arkan ever deployed to this area, everyone knew who Arkan was and that they were making a very, very dangerous bargain by engaging this person as part of the armed forces. The other thing that needs to be seen here, and it's reflected in the new military documents, is that the military is, of course, not very happy with and quite intolerant of armed formations that do not subject themselves to their chain of command. And at this point they are trying with mixed success to assert or, rather, resubordinate all so-called volunteer formations, including Arkan's formations, to the military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, on that point let's have 0247, please, Defence tab 12, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while we're --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Pardon. I apologise for the interruption, counsel. Just -- I was just listening to the two other channels, and again it's a highly complex discussion. Words are being said very swiftly, and I'm watching the court reporter, and I have the impression that people in the booth might be struggling a little bit to stay on top of it. And because it's a rather complicated subject matter, it might be useful just to keep in mind the pace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'll do my best. So I was calling 02437. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this concerns an attack on a place called Luzac, which is around the middle of November 1991. Does this reflect what you were just saying; namely, that not only are there attempts to subordinate Arkan's groups, Arkan's group, they are actually even expressly listed in the order of battles being undertaken by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to be careful here because I think you're asking me to comment on what, based on my initial reaction to the document, appears to be a page that is not a page produced by the Yugoslav authorities but rather from some kind of report that was filed before this Court either the OTP or the Defence. But I'm happy to agree with you that there were attempts to subordinate Arkan's group during the fall of 1991. Those attempts were unsuccessful. But there were also many operations, as far as I can see from the military reports, where the two co-operated side by side to general satisfaction for both the JNA and Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the origin of this document is attested to by a witness. And I don't propose to go into that with you. However, in light of what you said, I would nevertheless tender the document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think this is the appropriate witness to tender this document. You may -- well, I'm not going to go into who's the author and all - this is for my learned friends to know, but we have a military expert who will be testifying at a later stage. The witness does not -- hasn't seen the document before and cannot attest to the veracity of what's in there or can't comment about what units are being used, what is this attack on Luzac. So I think that the foundation is very weak at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This -- it will be coming up, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I withdraw the tendering of the document. Thank you, Mr. President. Could we have P152, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that actually you've referred to a couple of times now today. And this is Major-General Andrija Biorcevic, commander of the 12th Corps, and he awards small-arms as a war trophy to the most successful leaders of what he characterises the Serbian District of SBWS Territorial Defence as follows: Radovan Stojicic, Zivko Trajkovic, Zeljko Raznjatovic. Would you regard this as a further indication that Biorcevic views these individuals as subordinated to him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting that the TO is not under federal Yugoslav law subordinated to the JNA at the very least in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was responding to your very specific question, which is whether this document provides further indication that Biorcevic views these individuals as subordinated to him. There's nothing in this particular document that indicates that these persons were subordinated to Biorcevic. Other hand, there is the phrase most successful leaders of the Territorial Defence of the Serb District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. It is my experience both in examining documents from the SAOs and from Bosnia and Herzegovina that just because someone sees fit to award a trophy weapon to someone else, that does not necessarily indicate subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move to a new topic entirely, and this concerns the emergence of the conflict in Croatia. And you testified on page 2423 that, and I quote: "The very notion of an independent Croatian state was, even under the best of circumstances, likely to create enormous anxiety among at least a substantial portion of the Serb population in Croatia." And you also testified that the historical background to that anxiety was the fact that the only previous precedent of an independent Croatia was the independent state of Croatia created during World War II which you said adopted extremely discriminatory policies against Serbs, jews, and Roma and other minorities and, in your words, "culminated in a genocide against the Serbs and these other minorities on the territory of NDH." Is that correct? Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as indicated that is not only my view that is, I believe, an accurate reflection of the scholarly consensus regarding the so-called independent state of Croatia that existed from 1941-1945.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And at page 2423 you said that Franjo Tudjman had "dabbled in revisionism." Can you tell us what exactly he said that you would characterise as revisionism?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps you could just briefly elaborate on what you meant when you said that he dabbled in revisionism?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo Tudjman was, during a significant portion of his career, a professional historian who directed the institute for the history of the working movement or workers' movement, rather, in Zagreb. By approximately the early 1960s, he began to produce work, the gist of which was to probe what had happened during the the Second World War, during this so-called independent state of Croatia, and he began to suggest - very controversially - that despite its very nauseous policies, this state had, after all, been the reflection of a true desire of the Croat nation to have their own independent state. And so he gradually and in great depth elaborated this thesis stating that notwithstanding its genocidal policies, which he also then proceeded to minimalise, and I believe in many cases cast even into doubt, he stated that, We have to after all regard this as a success in that we got a state, we Croats obtained our own state. So there is something to be salvaged in this history of the independent state of Croatia. That thesis of his, which he elaborated in numerous works, was not only an anathema to the ruling Communists in Yugoslavia and therefore he was removed from his post, and he eventually also served a prison sentence in Croatia, but also earned him a reputation among many scholars and also later more popularly among Serbs in Croatia as a revisionist or denialist of the crimes that had been committed against Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you recall whether he said anything specific in terms of negating, denying, minimizing that these events had occurred? The genocide I mean.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to mention but one thing, he was among a number of Croat scholars who, in the 1980s in particular, tried to revise downwards significantly the number of Serbs who had perished in the concentration camp Jasenovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember what was the difference between the historical consensus as to how many victims there were there and Mr. Tudjman's view of that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the translation. The numbers that were used in the former Yugoslavia as this historiographical debate raged in the 1970s and 1980s, and I believe -- perhaps Your Honours are familiar with the term "historikerstreit" from Germany. This was a Serbo-Croat "historikerstreit," a dispute among historians with certain Serbs inflating the number to very large proportions and certain Croats by contrast reducing it as far as possible, I think even to below 60.000 at one point. And for that reason, there were attempts by what I would call more objective scholars, more reasonable scholars to re-examine all the evidence and come up with the most reliable figures, and they indeed produced a figure that was significantly higher than the figure that Mr. Tudjman was willing to entertain.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What is that figure?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I think -- and I don't have all of my sources in front of me, obviously. But as I said, based on my recollection at this moment, Tudjman at the very least had reduced the figure to, I think, 60.000 or below, which is significantly less than those scholars I would refer to as being more objective arrived at and by further logic much much less than the most -- well, for lack of a better term, nationalist Serb scholars on the other end of the spectrum had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What is the consensus now amongst historians as to the numbers who were killed?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the best numbers were those provided by the scholar Vladimir Zerjavic, and I do not have the exact number in my mind right now, but I believe it's at least above 250.000 if not above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you also testified when you were here last that Tudjman engaged in "inflammable political rhetoric." What did you have in mind when you referred to inflammable political rhetoric? Can you give us some examples of what he may have said.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I stated, Tudjman's views on the Second World War and, in particular, the policies of the independent state of Croatia towards the Serbs, Jews, and Roma, were very controversial and were, in the context of the changes going on in Croatia, quite inflammable. I would also note that Tudjman's - what shall we call it? - strong interest in the state symbols of Croat nationhood and statehood, including his fondness for uniforms, emblems that in many cases resembled those used by the Second World War puppet state, the independent state of Croatia, were also seen by not just Serbs but also by non-nationalist Croats as being controversial and provocative. And those, again, were therefore likely to create significant disquiet among the Serb population and made it difficult, if not impossible, for President Tudjman to position himself as someone who would be a leader of all citizens of Croatia regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see the clock, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell. I was thinking about adding 15 minutes to this session and 15 minutes to the next one so we can perhaps proceed like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that, and this is at page 2423: "The very notion of an independent Croatian state was even under the best of circumstances likely to cause enormous anxiety." And then you went on to testify that: "More Serbs might have been willing to accept the idea of an independent Croatia if," and I quote, "had the HDZ gone about propagating this policy in a more conciliatory manner. Again, this is, I have to say, speculation because the HDZ did anything but that." Now I've heard what you've just said in response to the previous two questions, and there's no reason to recapitulate that, but I was wondering if there's anything else that you have in mind aside from Franjo Tudjman's inflammatory rhetoric and genocide denial that, to you, was relevant to your answer there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we referred in January to Mr. Josip Boljkovac, the first minister of internal affairs of the Republic of Croatia, and he is one of a number of actors who have written memoires about this period and who, notwithstanding their involvement in the government that was created in 1990, have noted with regret and sadness that the HDZ as the ruling party, and president Tudjman in particular, were not willing to or not able to extend a conciliatory branch of reconciliation and friendship to the Serbs and that this -- therefore, as it were, turned many Serbs away from the possibility of accepting more autonomy for Croatia, if not outright independence for Croatia. I think because we are focussing very heavily on the Croat side, it also is, in the interests of objectivity, that we note that there were a number of scholars and intellectuals on the Serb side, both in Serbia proper and among Serbs in Croatia, who were, as it were, stoking the fire from the other side and also calling into question whether any mutual ethnic co-existence could be possible under a government that was led by the HDZ. But I think, as a matter of historical record, it is clear that the possibilities that did exist for the HDZ to try to make Serbs feel comfortable in Croatia were not exploited by that party and unfortunately certain actors in the party contributed to creating a very hostile atmosphere to Serbs in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just to underline, sir, we're not here to litigate the merits of one side or the other. The only purpose of my question is to understand what informed the reactions of -- in particular, Mr. Hadzic, which, of course, the Prosecution has been asserting in various ways in its case. And so that's the purpose -- that's the reason why I'm asking you these questions, just so you understand that. And would you agree with me that in terms of what is the origin or at least what starts the conflict - and I don't mean armed conflict, I mean political contact - is, in effect, the desire to change the status quo by the Croatian government from a republic to in effect, a fully independent state?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to quite simply avoid answering that question because I do not think that - and in fact I teach my students at university - that it's very unproductive to try and find out who started what, when. This is a -- the process of the disintegration of the Yugoslav state is incredibly complicated and there are many things -- many antecedents to what happened in 1990 that we can go back and follow. Just to mention one thing, the desire of Croatia and Slovenia to move towards independence had in and of itself been influenced by what they viewed, correctly or incorrectly, as an attempt by Serbia to impose a recentralisation of the federal Yugoslav state and revise the constitution that had existed since 1974 which had granted significant autonomy to the six socialist republics of Yugoslav. So it's very difficult to see where precisely it begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's' very fair point and I don't in any way disagree with you. The reason I asked you the question was because at page 2426 of your previous testimony, which you don't have in front of, the impression was created that perhaps the Serbs were starting six months before the adoption of the constitution to, in effect, militate for a greater autonomy which created the impression of a cause and effect or a sequence of events. But am I correct in understanding that in effect that's -- there's either no point or it's impossible to find an answer to that question; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We could go back another six months and find another point and another six months and find yet another point, but I had to start somewhere. Let me just state categorically that it is not the intent of my report to apportion blame for anything that transpired. My report is about stating what we can understand about the process in Croatia based on the available documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And also during your previous testimony at page 2428, you said that the referendum that was held in September -- August and September 1990 was self-selective on the part of the Serbs who were trying to conduct that referendum. Now would you agree with me that the reason why it was self-selective wasn't in order to inflate the -- those in favour of greater autonomy. It was simply because the Croatian government would have arrested anyone who had walked into an area where the police had the authority to do so?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not agree that that is the sole reason. That's certainly part of the reason, and as I noted some of this was done quite covertly. But I think there is a significant degree of self-selection here. It is my understanding, based on reading Mr. Petrovic's book, that no one, neither Mr. Petrovic or anyone else involved in this organisation process at the time on the Serb side, had any reasonable expectation that the Croats would support them in such a referendum. It was a moot point and why go about picking a fight at this point with the Croats. Why not instead demonstrate, which they then did, that there was robust support for remaining in Yugoslavia among the Serbs of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Regardless of the final numbers of the referendum, would you agree that that position, the support for greater autonomy as an anecdote or a reaction to the move towards independence, that the vast majority of Serbs would indeed have supported that greater autonomy under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated before, I think we have a chain reaction process that is set into place which, again, can be best summarised by that question I raised in January: Why should be I a minority in your country if you can be a minority in my country? The ethnic demographics, one need only look at the census from 1991 in Croatia or for that matter of fact, Bosnia, to realise that it was impossible both politically, legally, and demographically to create ethnically homogenous states. Once one or more actors started moving down that road, particularly given the past very negative experience of the Second World War that were being manipulated on both sides, it was a tragedy waiting to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But would you agree with me that it's possible to have a project of independence, autonomy, separation, whether it be on the Croatian side or on the Serbian side that doesn't necessarily involve ethnic discrimination?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In theory, yes. And, again, had everyone, for lack of a better term, been on their best behaviour and had this entire process been done with legal assurances, international observation, and full respect of various international and European conventions on civil and political rights, then things could have ended very differently. As we all know that's unfortunately not the case, and I think it's rather academic, unfortunately, to speculate about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the reason that I ask that question is because there is the topic, the issue of what kind of rhetoric is appropriate and what kind of rhetoric is designed to encourage discrimination. And -- and I would ask you in respect -- ask you about one specific example. Do you think that the amendment to the Croatian constitution in -- at the Christmas of 1990, I believe it is, in which Serbs were eliminated as a founding nation or a constituent nation of Croatia, whereas Croats became the sole recognised people, in a sense, with constitutional status, do you think that that encouraged -- or do you think that that was in any way attempting to discourage discrimination against Serbs?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I think, and I believe I wrote this in the report, is that it certainly reinforced, and among some Serbs created, for the first time the strong feeling that they were going to be second-class citizens in Croatia, that their rights would come after the rights of ethnic Croats. And in that sense, and I believe this is the opinion of a number of Croat politicians, I believe the former president of Croatia, Stjepan Mesic has gone on the record stating as much, that this was a mistake made by the Croatian leadership at the time. It was completely unnecessary. It would have cost them nothing to have kept the Serbs as a constituent nation in the constitution, that this was one of many signals that was -- that contributed to the disintegration of the relationship between Serbs and Croats in Croatia. I would also point out again that and -- and an additional significant concept that exists at this point is the notion of victimisation. And so while I understand that there was concern and displeasure among the Serbs that they were no longer a constituent nation among -- according to the constitution of the Republic of Croatia, it is conversely or was conversely a grave and in my eyes highly problematic exaggeration for Serb leaders in Croatia at the time, as some of them did, to assert that this was a road that was going to lead directly to the establishment of concentration camps for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see the clock now Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Before we take a break, let's see where we are going and what is possible. Mr. Gosnell, how long would you need to finish your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe another hour should be sufficient. I believe that I have an hour and a quarter, that was my prediction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The 15 minutes you have had now. So you still have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. So the 15 minutes you have had and there is still 60 minutes left, if we have to reserve 30 minutes for re-direct. Is that more or less what you expect, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will try to be as prompt as I can, Your Honours. Maybe even 20 minutes, but ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So then we'll take the break now until -- we come back at 1.00. And then we'll sit until 2.30 at the utmost. I think that would suit your travel plans, Mr. Nielsen; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm very grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to save time I can take care of a housekeeping matter, if I may. At page 62, line 25 of today's transcript, I erroneously referred to transcript page 2343. The proper transcript page is 2423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 6059, 65 ter 06059.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Dr. Nielsen, I hope you will forgive me. I'm going to jump around a little bit discursively between one topic and the next to make sure I approach things in the sequence that's most important for us, so I just wanted to let you know that. And I'm now calling up a document that was on neither party's list of exhibits but that you've now mentioned, I think, three times, and this is the letter from Mr. Hadzic to the town commander of Ilok. And it's dated the 23rd of December, 1991. And I'm correct in saying this is not referenced in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. Gosnell just before I respond to this document which I mentioned earlier, can I just say that so that I do not misinform the Court I just wish to very briefly revise the statement I made about the numbers of victims in World War II, in particular Jasenovac, because rather I, as I noted to Mr. Gosnell, didn't feel confident in stating such numbers spontaneously based on memory, I have a book with me that I consulted during the break and I would therefore like to briefly inform you and the Court that the figures cited by Mr. Tudjman for deaths in Jasenovac were I believe 20- to 30.000. That is lower even than I had stated. The figures that Zerjavic, who is regarded as one of the more objective historians on this point, lists for Jasenovac are 80- to 90.000. And that the high figures on the other end of the spectrum cited by certain Serb historians, for example Mr. Milan Bulajic, are over 600.000. So that gives you range. But I think the upshot of this whole discussion is that one could ask why in the context of Yugoslavia in 1990 it was even necessary to have such a discussion about such a painful topic. And I would again also mention that another, in my view, mistake by Mr. Tudjman was that he tried to rename the square for the victims of fascism in Zagreb into the square of Great Croats which also caused a great deal of controversy both among Serbs and Croats. Lastly, I would just point out that I have the 25th December document in front of me, not the 23rd December document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I believe the correct number should be 06055. I see my learned friend nodding. Well, before or while this document is coming up, Dr. Nielsen, I have one other small matter that I can address with you. And it was your reference to Arkan becoming a hot potato certainly by April 1992, and you may recall the last time we were here, I put it to you that some individuals might have had a tendency or the urge to use Arkan, references to Arkan, as a way of discrediting, in particular, Mr. Hadzic. And would you agree that in fact those two are related, that, indeed, by a certain date everyone was trying to wash their hands of Arkan and that indeed there was not a claim for Arkan or approval of Arkan, but that there was general disapproval and that tying him to, for example, Mr. Hadzic, was a way of discrediting, Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that a point arises at which many people, many actors view Arkan as a negative presence and that a number of these actors are trying to wash their hands of him, despite their previous approval of his actions. However, it is not my reading that the documents in which I see Mr. Hadzic's name mentioned together with Mr. Raznjatovic, or Arkan's name, were produced with the motivation or at least not solely produced with the motivation of discrediting Mr. Hadzic. I would also note that I was not able to find instances in which Mr. Hadzic who, I believe, was aware that other people were associating Arkan with him, I did not find any instances in which Mr. Hadzic publicly distanced himself or spoke disapprovingly of Mr. Raznjatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, for example, if we had an allegation from Milan Martic or for that matter from some -- any other politician who was seeking to discredit Mr. Hadzic, and a convenient way to do that would be to invoke Arkan as a close ally or friend or colleague or someone under the authority of Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if there's a specific case of such a mention of Arkan in his association with Mr. Hadzic that you are referring to made by Mr. Martic or anyone else, I'm happy to discuss that. But the ones that I cite in the section on Arkan, I do not see any, again, of -- one of those documents as being motivated solely or even primarily by a desire to disparage Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the document I have in mind, I don't propose to do to -- to go to it is the report, the DB report, which is based on a source whose initials you note in your report as VDZ. And I believe you've referred to that document before. Would you agree that where we're dealing with someone like that, there would, indeed, be a motivation to do just what I've said?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that such a motivation could exist particularly on the part of that person. And I believe that for precisely that reason that document needs to be read with that in mind and -- but again, also needs to be compared to numerous other documents in which an association between Mr. Hadzic and Arkan is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we look at page 2 of this document which is the one that you have referred to several times which is a letter to the town commander of Ilok, dated 23rd December, 1991. He says there at the top of the page in English: "I hope that you know that we did not for a moment challenge the army's presence in our area and its involvement in all matters, appreciating it to be a part of a comprehensive process from liberation, through stablisation of the area, to creating conditions for our ministries and civilian authorities to take over and assume full responsibility for their work. "Admittedly, we were never officially informed about the conditions under which the so-called military rule was established in a part of our Serbian district and what it really means in drawing a line between military and our jurisdiction, but the fact is that our efforts were often limited by citing its existence and conditions." Would you agree that what we seem to see here, and, of course, I'm sure that you -- your -- there's always a possibility of ulterior motives, but when you read this, do you have the impression that Mr. Hadzic is expressing some discontent with having been shut out by the army in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly think that there is some dissatisfaction expressed here. It is at least implicitly a criticism of the military when he states that he and the others on the civilian side were not officially informed about the conditions. I read that as a criticism of the military. Why was I not informed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And down at the bottom of the page 2 -- down at the bottom of page 2, it says: "We hope and expect our minister of finance to be given an opportunity to check the situation and the flow of funds on transfer accounts, hoping for your assistance in the matter, all the more so, since economic activity in Ilok was revived, in part through the direct engagement of military organs." And just to go down to the middle of page 3, and this is the last passage I'll bring to your attention: "The government has been told that the settling of Ilok went on rather well and that your commands was competent in all matters. Naturally, we are not bothered by this, but in the spirit of co-operation we would appreciate at least being informed about the criteria according to which it was done, with a possible remark that our approval does not go without saying." Do you have any observation in respect to that passage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When read together with the answer that Mr. Hadzic receives later from the military command in Ilok, it becomes clear that the military, on the one hand, and Mr. Hadzic and his government, on the other hand, have clashed over various matters on several occasions, that they have not even eye to eye on at least some matters, and they are referring to that somewhat elliptically but with the overall message that we now need to henceforth better co-ordinate our efforts so that these problems will not recur.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say in fact he is trying to use diplomatic language to mitigate or lessen what appears to be some kind of conflict with the JNA in terms of jurisdiction and just information about what's going on?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is, I think, indeed, trying, and largely succeeding in using diplomatic language to do as you indicate. Other hand, the military, perhaps as is the case with career military officers, is somewhat less diplomatic in indicating their disgruntlement with the way things have been running up to the present point in their letter two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I don't propose to take you to that letter, but that is a, in our opinion, a correct characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We would tender 65 ter 06055, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit D30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have to P37, which is Prosecution tab 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, this concerns the discussion that occurs at one of the SFRY Presidency meetings which you refer to at paragraph 206 of your report and which you discussed at page 2486 of your testimony. And this is about Mr. Hadzic's comments in respect of what you refer to as "the topic of forced removal of the civilian population." Now I'll just for it to come up. Could we have the B/C/S version, page 92; and the English version, page 68. That's -- that's nicely centred. Thank you. Dr. Nielsen, I was not clear as to what your actual interpretation is of Mr. Hadzic's words. Could you clarify what you think Mr. Hadzic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thank you for the opportunity to clarify this. I agree with you. I don't think I was very clear when we discussed this last time. Just to provide a bit of context because we cannot see it on this page, but immediately preceding Mr. Hadzic there is a long passage in which Radovan Karadzic speaks and he talks about the movement of peoples, and he refers - as I state in paragraph 206 - he asks, "Who will force the Croats from Vojvodina to go to Krajina. Those are nebulous ideas and the word is shocked by them, although India and Pakistan even did also such things. At this moment in Europe it is questionable whether that would be feasible." And to me that -- that is -- the point of departure that Karadzic is essentially saying, You know, at certain points in world history there have been mass movements of people and the world currently views that as abhorrent and it would be therefore doubtful that those kinds of movements would be feasible in Europe at this moment. And then when we get to Mr. Hadzic's comments, his first sentence is, at least the way I translated it, this is not nebulous. And then -- and it's very fragmentary in B/C/S, if we could -- could we have the translation scrolled down so I can see. These are -- I will just read the words that follow the sentence. "This is not nebulous. Serbs from Zagreb should resettle and Serbs from Belgrade, and now from this terrain," or "this area, there is" -- that is -- there's many ways you can translate it, "it is out of the question," "that's not to be discussed." But the part I would point out in the translation, the part when Mr. Hadzic says, "And now from this terrain" or "from this area" is missing from the English translation. So as the first order of business, I definitely would say that the statement that he makes, at least the second sentence of his statement, is at the very least ambiguous. But the first sentence to me is very clear. Mr. Karadzic or Dr. Karadzic has just said, "This is a nebulous idea," and Mr. Hadzic -- in referring to population movements, and Mr. Hadzic then says, "This is not nebulous."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm informed, Dr. Nielsen, that the word "from" does not appear in the B/C/S as being attributed to Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. It says -- but it uses the -- if I may be slightly technical, the genitive case, "of this terrain." As you well know, these stenographic records are in many cases imperfect, and indeed as we unfortunately, and again I apologise to the court reporter we see here, sometimes participants at these meetings or sessions speak so quickly that even a word or even a part of a sentence is bound to go lost. But I would again focus my attention, as I did in the report, on the first sentence of Mr. Hadzic's response, which -- where I don't think there's any ambiguity. I translated it as "that is not nebulous." The official translation we have here is, "There is nothing nebulous in it." And if we go back to Mr. Karadzic's statement, the only thing to which he can be referring is this notion of resettlement or population exchanges with -- with certain historical precedents mentioned by Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, just to try to take this shortly and to summarise, we have Dr. Karadzic allegedly saying it is rather questionable. And then we have Mr. Hadzic saying, No, it's not questionable. It's out of the question. It can't be done. That's not nebulous. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please have the previous page of the B/C/S? And I ... if we see in the English, it says, "First of all, the Serbs of Krajina must not be favoured here. On the contrary, they have to be stimulated to go back there." And then slightly later, we have the question: "But who is going to make the Croats from Vojvodina go to Krajina? These are nebulous ideas." "To su maglovit ideje." And my point is that the notion of what is or is not nebulous here, to me, when Mr. Hadzic responds, "There is nothing nebulous in it," to me that is a reaction to Mr. Karadzic's rhetorical question -- or his statement, "These are nebulous ideas." But I'm, again, happy to -- my point is to draw the attention of you and the Chamber to this exchange, and I think with the caveat that I think it might be worth asking for a revised translation, I -- I -- I would hope that everyone reads this and draws whatever conclusions they see fit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, looking at the entire context, is it your view that it -- that Mr. Hadzic is in any way advocating forcible transfer of civilian populations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reading, my view of this document is that Karadzic is saying historical circumstances and European public and political opinion mean that forcible transfer or exchange of civilian populations cannot occur and that Mr. Hadzic questions whether this is, indeed, true. That is my reading of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm going to give you my interpretation which involves the broader context of the entire passage. And when you read the entire passage, starting with, "I reckon," and there are even some earlier references, but we can see just from this page what is going on I submit to you. And what we see is that Dr. Karadzic is lamenting the departure of Serbs from the Krajina to Serbia and elsewhere which thereby, in his view, weakens the position of the Serbian minority in Croatia. And then he believes -- or then he discusses what I believe he suggests, Dr. Karadzic, that is, is a highly distasteful alternative which is -- which he believes has actually been proposed by the Croats, and that distasteful alternative is the full transfer of Croat and Serb populations between the SBWS or Croatia and Vojvodina. At least that's how I read his -- this -- when he refers to "they," when he say, "I mentioned this only to make you cognisant of their way of thinking," he must be referring to someone. Would you agree with me that in saying "their" he may be referring to the Croats?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And doesn't the interpretation I've just given accord with Mr. Hadzic's response which otherwise seems anomalous. He says, "Serbs from Zagreb and Belgrade should resettle"; in other words, we would like Serbs who have left or who are elsewhere to come to the Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that, first of all, we have agreed on -- by my count the vast majority of items that we've discussed. But on this particular instance I'm going to, for now, stand by my interpretation in page -- in paragraph 206 with, again, the observation that I think it's important that we all read this passage and draw our own conclusions. So as far as we are concerned, we're going to have agree that we disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's just focus on the top two paragraphs on this page where we see Dr. Karadzic saying that: "There should be a centralised service which would take care of the attainment of national goals. This service should be primarily linked to Krajina and should be economically motivated. I do not know much about the laws and maybe you have already discussed this matter, but when it comes to the investment legislation, the taxation, et cetera, I reckon that situation there will be more favourable so that there will be no need for companies from Serbia to send gifts there. They have to be motivated to develop things there based on ownership as the labour will be cheaper down there, the taxes will be lower, et cetera." Now, doesn't it seem to you that there Dr. Karadzic is saying let's figure out a policy that will encourage people to go back to this area from which many Serbs are leaving because they view it as an undesirable place to live?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree that that is -- where the discussion initially comes from, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you're not willing to allow that context to inform your interpretation of Mr. Hadzic's response?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we're on the topic of context, I'm also looking at this statement in the context of a much larger series of discussions that take place at these Presidency meetings and where the topic of forcible removal or more euphemistically expressed population exchange is not a -- is not -- is discussed frequently or at least at several meetings of this Presidency. And so that is part of the context overall that informs my reading of this passage. But as I stated, I think that I have my interpretation of this. You have your interpretation. And we'll have to leave it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Mr. Hadzic a party to those other meetings and conversations that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on some occasions, but I don't have the ability to tell you off the top of my head how many Presidency meetings he attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: None of those are mentioned in your report as substantiating your conclusion about Mr. Hadzic's words, are they?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I do not mention other Presidency meetings in this paragraph of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move to another topic, and that is paragraphs -- about 150 to 170 of your report, concerning police and the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And we're done with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by my count, there are exactly two documents that show that Mr. Hadzic issued any orders to the police in the RSK. Would you agree that that's the number?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is probably correct. I have definitely been able to note that there are very, very few instances of Mr. Hadzic issuing any orders to the police in the RSK, at least as we can determine based on the available documentation. I would, however, just remind the Court that at least according to Mr. Martic in the video that we viewed in January, the participation of the RSK MUP in the the corridor operation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the summer of 1992 also took place pursuant to instructions issued by Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On the instructions and the decision of the Supreme Defence Council of which Mr. Hadzic was a part; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume that's correct. I do not have the instructions or the decision. I was paraphrasing what Mr. Martic said at the event that we viewed on the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the two orders that we see that Mr. Hadzic is involved in concern on the one hand this issue of currency detailers - at least that's our position, your position was that it was narcotics dealers - and about securing the radio and television facilities of the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's referenced, for the record, at paragraphs 156 and 161 of your report. And would you agree with me that those are both areas that could be termed issues of national or strategic significance; namely, regulating currency flows and securing television and radio stations?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you mentioned, we have our outstanding disagreement on the first issue. But as regards the securing of the radio television company of RSK, I agree that in the eyes of the RSK authorities, control over the radio/television was a matter of strategic significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, actually, Dr. Nielsen, I recall that we didn't disagree at the end in respect of deliry [phoen]. You did concede that it could well have been a reference to currency speculators; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stated that it was one possible interpretation, and I recall that I also stated that the persons who were, based on my experience of examining police documents, involved in elicit currency dealing were typically also involved in other illegal activities, such as narcotics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you didn't exclude the interpretation that it may have been directed squarely and exclusively at currency speculators?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not exclude the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And would you say given your expertise as an analyst of police affairs specifically in the former Yugoslavia, that it's in no way surprising that the president of the republic would not be involved in giving operational instructions to the police?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just trying to see whether you posed the question in a negative or a positive way. I would state that based on my expertise, certainly in Bosnia and Herzegovina there are instances in which the president of the republic would be involved in giving operational instructions to the police. But that in the majority of cases, also in Bosnia-Herzegovina, those decisions tend to be issued through the competent minister of internal affairs and not by the president directly unless it involves urgent national security matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And whatever may be the case in respect of other republics, we don't see that in respect of Mr. Hadzic in the RSK, do we?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated, the available record, as you also described it, indicates that we have only those orders that you mentioned available to us that were issued by Mr. Hadzic directly to the police, and then with the caveat that you also mentioned, the instructions, orders, or whatever they may have been precisely, issued with respect to the operation in the corridor in the summer of 1992. So there is absolutely not a significant amount of documents that indicate that Mr. Hadzic directly issued orders to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in respect to that operation in the summer of 1992, you recognise, surely, that that's a military operation not a law enforcement or typical police operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The corridor operation was primarily a military operation, and, again, it is one of a number of cases in which various strategic considerations mean that the police are, for all intents and purposes, treated as an armed or combat force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When placed in combat; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When deployed in the primary function of defending what are identified as vital national interests of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Right. So none of these three orders emanating from Mr. Hadzic in any way reflect that he's involved in traditional law enforcement activities by the RSK police; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that after the establishment of the RSK, there are no indications, as I have been able to see it in the available documentation, that indicate that Mr. Hadzic is involved in law enforcement activities or other routine issues of internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to move to another topic which is a series of questions you were asked by the Prosecution about Bapska, and in particular whether it was the agenda of the SBWS government to take over municipalities that, as of 1941, had a Serb majority but may not have had such a majority in 1991. And at one point you testified at page 2451 that it would have -- "It would not surprise me if they had been to the archives and determined that, for example, Bapska had been a Serb majority area prior to 1941." And you were shown a list of population figures suggesting that the population of Bapska included only a relatively few Serbs? Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now isn't it possible in respect of Bapska, and let's just keep our focus on Bapska for the moment, that the reason that the jurisdiction was extended to Bapska is that it's surrounded on all sides by areas that are substantially majority Serb?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was an area, an enclave, as it were, if that is what you're suggesting, and I'm not familiar with the -- as I stated previously, the ethnic demographics of individual villages, settlements, or municipalities in this region, but if there was an indication that Bapska was an enclave of persons of ethnicity other than Serbian, surrounded by areas that, as you call it, were -- had substantial Serb majorities, then it would not surprise me that some of the actors involved in the military operations in the Autumn of 1991 would have taken a decision to include Bapska in the area over which they wished to exercise jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you'd agree, wouldn't you, that it's not even possible for Serb forces to enter the eastern part of SBWS without going through Bapska, from Serbian territory.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me to answer that, honestly I would have to have a map in front of me. So I'm willing to take your word for it, if -- if that is what you are stating, but I do not have a mental map of these settlements in my head. At least not Bapska in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you don't know where Bapska is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where Bapska is in terms of its location generally speaking, but I do not -- I cannot point to Bapska and tell you right now which particular area of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, or Srem it is in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you briefly about your reliance on Ilija Petrovic's book. And do you accept that his book is reliable as a whole? Are there parts that you consider less reliable? What's your general approach to that book and its reliability.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've answered that question quite precisely already. My whole -- my view on the book is that where he describes events in the region of Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem during the period that I examined, and where I have been able to see those events described elsewhere in other documents that were made available to me, it is my view that, in general, his recollection of those event seems to be quite in conformity with those other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you appear to place emphasis on the fact that you would accept Petrovic's accounts and information to the extent they are corroborated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My preference is, of course, always to have the ability to compare his accounts or anyone else's accounts to other sources. However, again, because of the deplorable state of documentation, there are a number of things that he or others describe that cannot be corroborated because we simply do not have documents about that particular incident. And in those cases, in the absence of such other documentation, and in the absence of an abundant number of instances in which his account does conflict with existing documentation, I included his version here making it clear, of course, that this stemmed from him as a source.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's just take a look at a few examples. At paragraph 21, your sole source for saying that Goran Hadzic was the president of -- I'm sorry, let me find the reference here. Yes. The sole source for your claim that Goran Hadzic was appointed president of the Serb National Council of the SBWS on the 17th of March, 1991, is, at paragraph 45, Ilija Petrovic's claim that's the case. You do include two or three other sources in that footnote but none of them are relevant to that claim; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The sources that I include are in respect of being able to corroborate, for example, his position within the SDS in Vukovar but not in -- in terms of his position as the president of -- or his role in the Serb National Council of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you think the fact that Ilija Petrovic correctly identified Goran Hadzic as a member of the Vukovar SDS Executive Board makes his claim that Goran Hadzic was the president of the the Serbian national council more likely? Is that your proposition?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think you are mischaracterising what I just stated. I'm not making any judgement about Ilija Petrovic's correctness or lack of correctness in identifying Mr. Hadzic in that particular function based on the fact that Petrovic correctly identifies Mr. Hadzic's role in the -- alone in the SDS Executive Board, but again based on a number of additional other events which Mr. Petrovic does explain correctly. This is not the sole instance in which Mr. Petrovic says something that I have been able to corroborate elsewhere. In this particular case, I do not have any other corroboration for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And despite being president apparently, as discussed in paragraph 22, Goran Hadzic's approval was not required for the declaration of autonomy because as we know at the time that declaration was issued he was in the hospital; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. He was in the hospital after the events at Plitvice Jezera.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And concerning paragraph 23, which I presume you would agree was a very important letter from the Serbian national council to the SFRY Presidency seeking assistance, dated the 28th of May, that document was not signed by Goran Hadzic. It was signed by Ilija Petrovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have the document in front of me, but, yes, I believe that, as I state here in paragraph 23, it was Ilija Petrovic who was writing on behalf of the Serb National Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, footnote 48 clearly says: "Forwarding letter of Ilija Petrovic at 28 May, 1991," correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, written -- so writing on behalf of the Serb National Council, Ilija Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So Goran Hadzic as the president of the Serb National Council is not involved in the declaration of autonomy of March 31st, and there's no indication he's involved in this letter of the 28th of May, 1991, is there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you ever get the impression that in respect of some of the documents that are appended in Mr. Petrovic's book that he might simply have been sitting at a type writer and producing documents to aggrandise his own role in events?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Petrovic is certainly a person who is very fond of highlighting his own role in events in this area and in these political procedures that lead to the establishment of a Serb Autonomous District. Again, I have, at least based on the documents that I have been able to examine, not found an indication of a -- an instance in which Mr. Petrovic has produced a document that I would be able to, based on other documents, adduce to be a forgery. If that's what you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you noticed that many of the documents that are attached to his book are not gazetted?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I would also note that based on my requests for the gazettes of the Serb Autonomous District, as far as I recall, the collection of Serb Autonomous District gazettes that is in the possession of the OTP is incomplete. We do not, as far as I know, have the full collection of the gazettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, on what basis do you assert that it's not complete?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis that, at least looking at the numbers of the gazettes that I received, when I requested the gazettes from the OTP, I do not recall that I received every single number so that I could build a full collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that there are a great number of footnotes in your report that rely exclusively on Ilija Petrovic's book?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There are a great number of instances in which I did rely on Ilija Petrovic's book, for the reasons that I have previously stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Namely, the inadequate state of documentation?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: One issue that you didn't discuss in your report or at least not with any degree of specificity is what was going on in the police in the lead-up, in the Croatian police in the lead-up to August 1991. Is there any reason why that was not part your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer just as a rather brief background to the fact that there were tensions in the Croatian police and that a number of people, for example, in paragraph 8, I refer to the Croatian police were deploying to police stations in areas populated by a Serb majority. And I refer to the suspension of several employees of the public security station in Knin; that is, the actions that the Croatian police chose to take to thwart what they viewed as illegal attempts to organise an exclusively Serb rule on certain territories of the Republic of Croatia. However, I did not produce - and it was not within the ambit of this report - to produce a section on the ministry of internal affairs of the Republic of Croatia for the period from the multi-party elections in Croatia until the outbreak of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: One thing that you do opine on, somewhat obliquely at times is, the reasonableness, for example, of Ilija Petrovic raising the specter of the HDZ wishing to establish a regime bearing certain similarities to the independent state of Croatia. And I believe you suggest that's -- that was irresponsible on his part. Wouldn't you agree that in making that suggestion you're relying on assessments about what changes were or were not occurring in the police at that time?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you would direct me to a specific portion in the report, then I'm happy to comment on that. However, as we dealt with -- right before the previous break, we dealt with at length my views of the irresponsible activities of various actors on the Croatian side, including the president, and I would also state in that, including certain officials in the police, that -- I -- I do not have a difficulty accepting that the police in Croatia, that is ethnic Croats in the police in Croatia, were using the police to try to move towards an autonomous or independent Croatia and that the police in Croatia played an important and, indeed, crucial role in the formation of an independent Croatian state. Where I believe I differed with Mr. Petrovic, and again I'm speaking a bit from memory here, is that Mr. Petrovic on at least one occasion in his book seems to indicate or believe that Croats, police officers, were drawing up lists of persons who would be executed or incarcerated from the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you would agree that there was very serious cause for alarm, given the basis of events that were going on, in particular, in the Croatian police in early 1991. If you were a Serb.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree that there was very serious cause for alarm. Given the basis of events that were going during that period, and I believe that I also stated that quite clearly earlier today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you'd agree that it would be reasonable under those circumstances to, as a politician, openly discuss political solutions that would reassure the population; correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although that begs the question of what are political solutions that would reassure the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, of course it's very hazardous to speak about entire movements, but at times you have testified - and you did testify last time - that politicians manipulated public opinion in the SBWS. You didn't say that Goran Hadzic manipulated public opinion. But would you agree with me that there were those and it was perfectly possible to espouse a desire for autonomy, greater independence, authority over policing, as a meaningful response to what was going on in early 1991?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that in terms of the second half of 1990 or early 1991, there were -- there was a possibility to discuss how policing was going to be structured. There were many discussions, for example, about ensuring that the police in various municipalities in Croatia should reflect the ethnic distribution of the population in those municipalities. There were also, at least theoretically, possibilities for discussing how the police could be controlled in a way that if such a way were indeed possible and the possibilities for that were rapidly disappearing as time advanced, in a way that both, for example, Belgrade, Zagreb, and Serbs in Croatia would be satisfied with it.
