And I would also agree that at least until the events in Borovo Selo, if we are to take Josip Bojkovac's word for it, and I stress this is based on the minister of internal affairs of Croatia's memoirs, according to his memoirs Mr. Hadzic was among those who were involved in such discussions until the events at Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will try to be as brief as possible to make sure that can you catch your plane this afternoon. So let me get right to it. Today -- no, sorry, in January during the first day of cross-examination, my learned friend was asking you about your access to OTP databases in the context of the methodology applied in preparing your report, if you recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This was at page 2532 for everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I would like you to explain to the Chamber, just for the sake of completeness, what other, if any, sources did you use for the preparation of your report and in the information gathering efforts?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all I would be remiss if I did not thank Mr. Gosnell and his co-counsel for the very stimulating questions that they posed. So thank you for that. As I stated earlier, I believe that in addition to the access that I had to OTP databases that I used in preparing my report, I also used a number of books that I identified, for example, the book by Nikica Baric, in preparing this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And -- yes. As an expert on history and police-related matters, how would you qualify your reliance on documents provided by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the point of view of methodology, I -- I was of necessity reliant upon the documents provided by the Office of the Prosecutor simply because with the possible exception of certain still unaccessible archives in the former Yugoslavia, there is no repository of relevant documentation that I have access to besides that which the OTP possesses. But I would also state, as I believe I did earlier, that in all cases, in -- when I did identify documents that I thought were relevant or were missing from the documents in -- that I had initially obtained from the OTP, I was in touch with the OTP and asked for those documents to be provided for me if they were available if I could not myself retrieve them from the EDS database.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Now on this issue of availability of documentation, this is an issue that was raised by the Defence at page 2537 in January, and you were asked about the confidence that you placed in the conclusions reached in your report having considered, and I quote from Mr. Gosnell, "the combination of a very sparse documentary foundation with the exclusion of witness evidence." At the time you were discussing the fact that you did not rely on witness evidence. Now, this was asked to you in a general matter without -- manner, sorry, without referencing specific parts of your report, and I would like you to look at the table of contents of your report. I don't know if you have a copy with you.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this is, just for reference, 65 ter 2837. I believe the table of contents is at page 2. And I'd like to remind you that at page 2506, during your examination-in-chief, when you were asked whether you had seen documents relating to the organisational structure of the MUP and the RSK or the SBWS, your answer was that as far as the SBWS was concerned, the documentation was very, very sparse. Now looking at the table contents, I would like you to look at Roman numeral number II, the general historical and political background. Could you tell the Chamber for this chapter how you would qualify the availability of sources relating to the general and historical background?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as we see Roman numeral II consists of four points, and the state of the documentation is such, if I were to rank the various SAOs hierarchically, the state of documentation for the SAO Krajina is by far the best in terms of its completeness and in terms of its availability, followed by the amount of documentation available for the SAO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, and by far the worst or most lacking set of documentation is that pertaining to the SAO Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And putting aside for a moment MUP-related matters, how would you qualify the availability of sources in relation to the historical background of the conflict in the early 1990s?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are speaking of the entire political context of the conflict in the early 1990s, then, the source base, I think, is -- is quite good, not least because a number of key discussions took place in Belgrade and those have been made available in -- in the form of stenographic records from meetings of, for example, the Federal Presidency. However, if we look at the meetings that took place, the discussions that we know must have transpired in, for example, the SAO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, then we possess very few sources that stem directly from those meeting, and therefore I had to rely primarily on the available gazetted decisions and, of course, the book of Mr. Petrovic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I will not go through each -- each chapter of your report one by one, but perhaps could you confirm for the Trial Chamber when you were talking about the fact that you had -- that the documentation was very sparse, which -- which chapter or section of your report would you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, I refer to my context as counsel for the Defence has -- has pointed out, my context is that I come to this subject from preparing an expert report previously on the MUP of Republika Srpska. And when one is used to such an abundance of sources as are existing for the MUP of Republika Srpska, then the available sources for the Krajina area of Croatia are, by contrast, already quite sparse. But as I noted, even within the available sources for the entities created by the Croatian Serbs, the vast majority of available sources pertain to the SAO Krajina and, later, to the RSK MUP, whereas -- and even during the RSK MUP phase to the Knin or western Krajina area and very -- by contrast relatively little documentation exists that enables one to reconstruct what transpired in the SAO SBWS and Western Slavonia. I think it is indicative that both in the direct examination and in the cross-examination we spent by my count the vast majority of the time discussing documents that were more recently obtained from the Serbian military archives, many of which cast great considerable additional light on this subject and that -- that -- that those 370-odd documents give us so much additional information says a lot about how little we had before they arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And looking at the last chapter of your report which we -- deals with the co-operation between the police of Serb-controlled entities in Croatia and the MUP of Serbia, again, how confident are you in relation to the availability of material in relation to that chapter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there we are assisted by the fact that a substantial amount of that documentation has become available more recently as Belgrade has been more generous with permission to its -- to access its archives, but I also have to state, again, that based on the number of reports we have and something we discussed repeatedly, the numbering of reports, one can easily as an analyst conclude that there must be many many more relevant reports in Belgrade that, if they exist, have not yet been provided to this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, this morning, I'm moving to another topic now, we spent a considerable amount of time dealing with Exhibit P194.140 which was Goran Hadzic's order appointing Arkan as commander of the TO training centre in Erdut, and this was on page 46 and 47 of today's transcript. Now, in one of the questions put to you by my learned friend, he referred to the fact that there's an absence in relation to the origin of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the Trial Chamber's information, there was a request from the Defence to -- to find out what was the origin of this document to the Office of the Prosecutor, and the OTP did inform the Defence that this was obtained from the Defence team of the -- of Jovica Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you note that -- several times that the authorities at the time were not very meticulous in their way of drafting documents, reports, letters, et cetera, and I would like you to look at Exhibit D30 which was just shown to you by my learned friend. This is the letter of the 23rd of December, 1991, by Goran Hadzic to the town commander in Ilok. And it's Exhibit D30. And if we look at that cover page, first page, sorry, can you, first of all, tell us if there is a number on this document?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As previously stated, there is no document number here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you are aware, and we will come to that in a moment, that there was a response to this document, to this letter.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. That response came on the 25th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While we're on this document, I would like you to turn to page 3 in the English version, which, by my calculations, should be page 2 in the B/C/S version. And this is a paragraph that my learned friend referred to which starts with: "The government has been told that the settlement of Ilok went on rather well." Are you able to locate that paragraph, Dr. Nielsen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the sentence here says that: "Naturally we're not bothered by this, but in the spirit of co-operation, we would appreciate at least being informed about the criteria according to which it was done, with a possible remark that our approval does not go without saying." Now, this last of the sentence, what is Goran Hadzic suggesting here, in your view, when he says that our approval does not go without saying?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read it as, first, Mr. Hadzic suggesting that they do need to arrive at joint criteria, that they take umbrage at the fact that they have not been informed what criteria are being used, but that he's also asserting his own authority in stating that just because the military has a certain criteria or because the military propose a certain criteria, this does not necessarily mean that the SAO district government will accept those criteria, that they may have to negotiate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And looking two paragraphs down, the paragraph beginning with: "In connection with this," here it appears that -- well, it does not appear, it is written that Hadzic informs the town commander that the government adopted a decision during a session of the government granting temporary residence to these persons. Now, again in relation to the previous answer you just gave, what can you say about how the government viewed its decision-making on these matters.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, as I see it, especially in light of what the military subsequently writes. There had been a number of instances where the military had expressed dissatisfaction with decisions made by the district and vice versa, and in the spirit of better co-operation, they are now trying to initiate a more direct dialogue so that they can engage in solving these problems together. As also discussed, this is in the general context at this time where the military has repeatedly expressed its desire to divest itself of matters that it views as better relocated to civilian authorities, and obviously from the point of view of the district it is of -- in their interest to assert control over such activities and to demonstrate that they can carry them out properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now let's look at the answer, which is at 65 ter 6059. And again as pointed out by my learned friend, these two documents were not on our lists but I think we have agreement on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not actually sure that we have an agreement, and I -- I apologise if I may appear to be not be taking a consistent position. It's just that now I'm in a position where I don't have an opportunity to look at this document with Dr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, this is a document that was referred to as you mentioned -- as the Defence mentioned three times by Dr. Nielsen this morning. Mr. Gosnell decided to show the letter that Goran Hadzic sent to the town command, and what I wish to do here is to show the response to complete the picture of what was that relationship between the government and the town command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would withdraw the objection if I would be granted some latitude, depending on the questions, to ask one or two follow-ups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So this is 65 ter 6059. Dated 25th of December, you can see at the top left it reads: "Reply to your letter." And it is addressed to Mr. Goran Hadzic. In the English version -- well, we can see the introduction on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the second page, please, of the English version, which -- I believe in the B/C/S version we'll have to scroll down to the bottom. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Nielsen, do you see the paragraph which begins: "I must admit that I expected ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Here, there's a discussion going on about how to deal with the issue of -- in resolving the issue of a settlement of refugees from other parts of the country. And if you could see in the middle of that paragraph, at least in the English version - we may need to go to the next page in the B/C/S version. It says here: "I am disappointed to have to say and inform you that the people you entrusted with the resolution of the most important civilian matter at the moment have not demonstrated any shred of necessary skills, resourcefulness, knowledge, and most devastating of all, good will." Now, what is the town commander informing Goran Hadzic of at this stage?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously the town commander is, first of all, expressing at the beginning of the paragraph his disappointment that the government authorities of the district had not acted as quickly in dealing with the settlement issue as the military might have desired. And then he goes on to state that these assumptions not having been borne out that the civilian authorities would do this. He was also disappointed in those cases where persons were appointed to deal with the -- what he calls the most pressing civilian matter, those persons were not capable and did not perform in a way that the military regarded as being positive. I would just point out that in the B/C/S original it talks about a lack of will. Good well is not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Lack of well. Okay. We'll submit that for a revised translation. And Dr. Nielsen, if we go to page 3 in the English version, my learned friend read to the part of Goran Hadzic's letter which stated that they are not contesting -- the government is not contesting the presence of the army. And you can see the beginning of that paragraph in the middle of the page: "As you are not contesting the presence of the army in the area, this leads to the conclusion that the army is there not because it is a zone of combat activity and because it is carrying out combat tasks but because you are graciously allowing it to be there." Now, how do you read this comment, that the government is graciously allowing the army to be there in light of the other documents that you have seen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's -- it's -- to me it's a puzzling statement, not least because he then goes on to state that everyone knows that the army arrived before the authorities of the Serb district. So I have no idea whether he is trying to sound facetious or not, but it is certainly the case that the army arrived in many cases before the district authorities, and this term of "graciously permitting us to be there," again, to me, it simply sounds facetious.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now by this stage, and this is something that I believe Goran Hadzic in his letter indicated earlier, that military operations were a thing of the past, and these are letters -- an exchange of lettering at the end of December 1991. Again, in relation to all the documents that you have seen and having regard to the fact that this is at a stage where combat activities are not ongoing, are you able to say anything about the government's position in relation to the presence of the army on its territory at the end of 1991 and early 1992?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I would like to make any general comment other than that, as previously discussed, there seems to be some consensus which is not without tension and indeed continues to be with quite tense into the spring of 1992 where the army wishes to divest itself of civilian matters but, at the same time, views with suspicion and, at times, disappointment, the efforts being made by the civilian authorities to take over the burden of performing those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were mentioning that this may have sounded a bit facetious on the part of Colonel Belic. If we go to the bottom of page 4 in the English version, and we may have to move to page 3 in the B/C/S version, if you look at the bottom of the page in the English version, it says here: "Mr. President, in order to overcome these problems," et cetera et cetera, "I place my command at your disposal with the wish for life to be restored to normal as soon as possible." And again, I mean, what can you make out of this exchange of letters between Hadzic and Belic in terms of what their relationship seems to be and again in light of what the army is saying here? They're placing their command at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to make, on the one hand, too much out of these two letters. It is one exchange of letters, though it is a very important one because we also don't have a lot of other such exchanges that go directly between an army command and Mr. Hadzic. But, again, is the case that there have been, as we see in many other documents, an abundant number of irregularities in this area, and they have now decided - this military officer and Mr. Hadzic - to initiate a written dialogue with a goal of better co-operation in the future. As a more general comment, the unfortunate aspect of the totality of the military documentation that stretches into the spring of 1992 is that it in many cases makes clear that these irregularities persisted for quite some months and that also there are no clear indications at all that anyone, paramilitaries, civilian leaders, military leaders, or otherwise were held to account before a court of law or in any other way for the irregularities that had taken place in the preceding period, including as regarded the resettlement issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have one last topic which will last two, three, minutes. If I may have your indulgence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: A very different topic. Dr. Nielsen, this morning you were also asked about the number of orders issued by Goran Hadzic to the Ministry of Interior. This was at page 84 of today's transcript where you answered in the following way: "It is correct that after the establishment of the RSK there are no indications, as I have been able to see it, in the available documentation that indicate that Mr. Hadzic is involved in law enforcement activities or other routine issues of internal affairs." Now as an expert on police institutions in the former Yugoslavia, if Goran Hadzic as president of the RSK did not involve himself as you say personally in law enforcement or other routine internal affairs issues, is this an indication that he did not have the authority or the power to intervene or involve himself in such matters?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I refer in the report to the constitutional powers that are vested in Mr. Hadzic in his capacity of president of the RSK. I believe that's on pages 17 and 18 of my report. And certainly as regards his abilities to propose members of the government and to proclaim laws by decree, for example, also one could argue to a lesser extent by even giving awards and recognitions, Mr. Hadzic did have the ability to influence the ministry of internal affairs. As to whether he exercised and how often he exercised those constitutionally-given powers, that is another matter. I would very quickly, however, point out that I at least on one occasion in the report refer to conflicts involving personnel disputes in the police in the RSK after it was formed in February 1992 where at least some of the actors involved tried to get Mr. Hadzic to be involved as a mediator in resolving those very pronounced personnel conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I note the time, Your Honours. This concludes my re-examination. I believe that we can leave to tomorrow morning the issue of the admission of the report and the exhibits given that Dr. Nielsen has to depart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: All right. If there's nothing else for Dr. Nielsen ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, this brings your testimony to an end. You're now released as a witness. We thank you very much for coming to The Hague one more time, and we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I may thank Your Honours for your indulgence, as well as those of the interpreters and everybody else in and around the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.32 p.m.,
